claim: Cryo-EM single-particle analyses typically require target macromolecule concentration at 0.05~5.0 mg/ml.
source: Cryo-EM single-particle analyses typically require target macromolecule concentration at 0.05~5.0 mg/ml, which is often difficult to achieve.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cryo-EM requirements in the abstract.

claim: MagIC-cryo-EM enables direct structural analysis of targets captured on magnetic beads, reducing the targets' concentration requirement to <0.0005 mg/mL.
source: Here, we devise Magnetic Isolation and Concentration (MagIC)-cryo-EM, a technique enabling direct structural analysis of targets captured on magnetic beads, thereby reducing the targets' concentration requirement to <0.0005 mg/mL.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MagIC-cryo-EM was adapted to a Chromatin Immunoprecipitation protocol to characterize structural variations of linker histone H1.8-associated nucleosomes isolated from interphase and metaphase chromosomes in Xenopus egg extract.
source: Adapting MagIC-cryo-EM to a Chromatin Immunoprecipitation protocol, we characterized structural variations of the linker histone H1.8-associated nucleosomes that were isolated from interphase and metaphase chromosomes in Xenopus egg extract.
evidence: This describes the experimental application of the method, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: DuSTER is a particle curation method that excludes low signal-to-noise ratio particles.
source: Combining Duplicated Selection To Exclude Rubbish particles (DuSTER), a particle curation method that excludes low signal-to-noise ratio particles
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the description and application of DuSTER in Figure 4.

claim: The 3D cryo-EM structures of nucleoplasmin NPM2 co-isolated with linker histone H1.8 were resolved, revealing distinct open and closed structural variants.
source: we also resolved the 3D cryo-EM structures of nucleoplasmin NPM2 co-isolated with the linker histone H1.8 and revealed distinct open and closed structural variants.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by structural data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: In conventional plunge vitrification method, 3 µL of aqueous samples greater than 1 mg/mL are typically required to acquire sufficient numbers of particle images on cryo-EM micrographs for 3D structure reconstruction.
source: In a conventional plunge vitrification method, 3 µL of aqueous samples greater than 1 mg/mL are typically required to acquire sufficient numbers of particle images on cryo-EM micrographs for 3D structure reconstruction (Table 1 Bhella, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bhella, 2019 and comparison in Table 1.

claim: Most of the target complexes in the sample solution applied on a cryo-EM grid must be removed by a blotting paper to make a thin ice layer suitable for analysis.
source: This is because most of the target complexes in the sample solution applied on a cryo-EM grid must be removed by a blotting paper to make a thin ice layer suitable for analysis.
evidence: This explains a fundamental limitation of conventional cryo-EM methods based on established knowledge.

claim: Affinity grids are amenable for lower concentration samples (~0.05 mg/mL).
source: Affinity grids, such as Ni-NTA lipid monolayer grids (Kelly et al., 2008), chemically functionalized grids (Llaguno et al., 2014), antibody-attached grids (Yu et al., 2016), and streptavidin monolayer grids (Wang et al., 2008), are amenable for lower concentration samples (~0.05 mg/mL)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on affinity grids.

claim: More than 300 proteins directly bind to the histone core surface.
source: more than 300 proteins directly bind to the histone core surface (Skrajna et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Skrajna et al., 2020.

claim: The averaged structures of the nucleosome core particle (NCP) in interphase and metaphase chromosomes are essentially identical to the NCP crystal structure assembled with histone proteins and DNA with strong nucleosome positioning sequences.
source: We found that the averaged structures of the nucleosome core particle (NCP) in interphase and metaphase chromosomes are essentially identical to the NCP crystal structure assembled with histone proteins and DNA with strong nucleosome positioning sequences (Luger et al., 1997; Chua et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by citations.

claim: The major structural variation of the nucleosome structures between interphase and metaphase chromosomes was attributable to the binding status of the oocyte-specific linker histone H1.8.
source: We also observed that the major structural variation of the nucleosome structures between interphase and metaphase chromosomes was attributable to the binding status of the oocyte-specific linker histone H1.8.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work cited as Arimura et al., 2021.

claim: The 3D structure of the H1.8-bound nucleosome isolated from metaphase chromosomes was resolved but not from interphase chromosomes.
source: We were able to resolve the 3D structure of the H1.8-bound nucleosome isolated from metaphase chromosomes but not from interphase chromosomes (Arimura et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: H1.8 in metaphase is most stably bound to the nucleosome at the on-dyad position, in which H1 interacts with both the entry and exit linker DNAs.
source: The resolved structure indicated that H1.8 in metaphase is most stably bound to the nucleosome at the on-dyad position, in which H1 interacts with both the entry and exit linker DNAs (Bednar et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2021; Dombrowski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous structural data and multiple citations.

claim: Stable H1 association to the nucleosome in metaphase likely reflects its role in controlling the size and the shape of mitotic chromosomes through limiting chromatin accessibility of condensins.
source: This stable H1 association to the nucleosome in metaphase likely reflects its role in controlling the size and the shape of mitotic chromosomes through limiting chromatin accessibility of condensins (Choppakatla et al., 2021)
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to Choppakatla et al., 2021.

claim: Nanobeads were easily identified on the grid as black dots in the intermediate-magnification montage map.
source: Nanobeads were easily identified on the grid as black dots in the intermediate-magnification montage map (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1B.

claim: Poly-nucleosome fibers were observed around the nanobeads in high-magnification micrographs.
source: In the high-magnification micrographs, poly-nucleosome fibers were observed around the nanobeads as expected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1C.

claim: The 3D structure of the nucleosome at sub-nanometer resolution was successfully determined using nucleosome-like particles selected from 550 micrographs.
source: Using nucleosome-like particles selected from 550 micrographs by the machine-learning-based software Topaz (Bepler et al., 2019a), we successfully determined the 3D structure of the nucleosome at sub-nanometer resolution (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: An intense halo-like scattering covered an ~30 nm radius around the nanobeads, interfering with the signal from particles that were proximal to the beads.
source: This result, however, revealed a notable issue; an intense halo-like scattering covered an ~30 nm radius around the nanobeads (Figure 1D, blue areas), interfering with the signal from particles that were proximal to the beads.
evidence: This is an observation from the pilot experiment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A protein spacer module was attached to the beads so that the target biomolecules are placed outside the reach of the halo.
source: To reduce the effect of the halo-like scattering surrounding the nanobeads, a protein spacer module was attached to the beads so that the target biomolecules are placed outside the reach of the halo (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a methodological solution implemented in the study, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The spacer module comprises an 11 nm triple helical bundle (3HB) protein and four copies of a 60 nm single alpha helix (SAH) protein.
source: After several rounds of optimization using the in vitro reconstituted H1.8-bound nucleosome as a model target, we chose a spacer module comprising an 11 nm triple helical bundle (3HB) protein (Huang et al., 2014) and four copies of a 60 nm single alpha helix (SAH) protein (Sivaramakrishnan and Spudich, 2011) for its effectiveness and reasonable production yield (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by optimization data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distal end of the spacer module was engineered to allow for exchangeable target-capturing modules by SPYcatcher-SPYtag conjugation.
source: The distal end of the spacer module was engineered to allow for exchangeable target-capturing modules by SPYcatcher-SPYtag conjugation (Figure 2B; Zakeri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a design feature supported by citation and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: H1.8-GFP-bound nucleosomes were isolated at a concentration of 1.7 nM (0.00047 mg/mL) from a mixture with a large excess of unbound mono-nucleosomes (53 nM, 0.012 mg/mL).
source: we isolated H1.8-GFP-bound nucleosomes by anti-GFP nanobody coupled to the MagIC-cryo-EM beads from a mixture of H1.8-GFP nucleosomes (1.7 nM, or 0.00047 mg/mL) and a large excess of unbound mono-nucleosomes (53 nM, or 0.012 mg/mL; Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The target concentration used was approximately 100–1000 times lower than the concentration required for conventional cryo-EM methods, including affinity grid approaches.
source: This target concentration was approximately 100–1000 times lower than the concentration required for conventional cryo-EM methods, including affinity grid approaches (Kelly et al., 2008; Llaguno et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to established methods supported by citations.

claim: Magnetic capture step significantly increased the number of beads that were found in the sample holes of the grid.
source: This magnetic capture step significantly increased the number of beads that were found in the sample holes of the grid (Figure 2F–I)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F–I.

claim: The spacer module successfully placed nucleosome-like particles outside the halo-like scattering surrounding the nanobeads.
source: High-magnification micrographs of MagIC-cryo-EM beads show that the spacer module successfully placed nucleosome-like particles outside the halo-like scattering surrounding the nanobeads (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by visual evidence in Figure 2J.

claim: Approximately 100 H1.8-GFP nucleosome particle images per bead were efficiently collected even with a sample concentration as low as 0.00047 mg/mL of H1.8-GFP nucleosomes in the heterogeneous sample.
source: Indeed, approximately 100 H1.8-GFP nucleosome particle images per bead were efficiently collected even with a sample concentration as low as 0.00047 mg/mL of H1.8-GFP nucleosomes in the heterogeneous sample (Figure 2J right panel).
evidence: This is quantitative data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Among the nucleosome-containing particles, 55.7% of them were classified as a nucleosome with H1.8 at the on-dyad position.
source: Among the nucleosome-containing particles, 55.7% of them were classified as a nucleosome with H1.8 at the on-dyad position (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is quantitative data from image processing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The final 3D structure of H1.8-bound nucleosome was determined at 3.6 Å resolution.
source: yielding a final 3D structure at 3.6 Å resolution (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is structural data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: MagIC-cryo-EM only required 5 ng of H1.8-GFP-bound nucleosomes (including 2 ng of DNA) per cryo-EM grid.
source: Notably, this method only required 5 ng of H1.8-GFP-bound nucleosomes (including 2 ng of DNA) per cryo-EM grid, which is comparable to or even lower than the requirements of widely used ChIP-seq (Zou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of sample requirement compared to ChIP-seq.

claim: The amount of nucleosome-associated H1.8 in interphase is reduced to approximately 30% of that in metaphase.
source: Despite the high accumulation of H1.8 in the nucleus (Maresca et al., 2005; Figure 3B), the amount of nucleosome-associated H1.8 in interphase is reduced to approximately 30% of that in metaphase (Arimura et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work cited as Arimura et al., 2021.

claim: The linker histone H1 has high mobility on chromatin.
source: Given the high mobility of the linker histone H1 on chromatin (Choppakatla et al., 2021; Willcockson et al., 2021; Yusufova et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The relative distributions of five nucleosome classes were largely similar between interphase and metaphase.
source: Overall, the relative distributions of these five classes were largely similar between interphase and metaphase (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The structures of H1.8-bound nucleosomes in interphase and metaphase were indistinguishable.
source: and the structures of H1.8-bound nucleosomes in interphase and metaphase were indistinguishable (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The structures of GFP-tagged H1.8-bound nucleosomes isolated from Xenopus egg extract chromosomes are essentially identical to the endogenous H1.8-bound nucleosome structure previously determined.
source: The structures of GFP-tagged H1.8-bound nucleosomes isolated from Xenopus egg extract chromosomes are essentially identical to the endogenous H1.8-bound nucleosome structure we previously determined Arimura et al., 2021.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous structural data.

claim: Differential positional preferences of H1.8 on the nucleosome are unlikely to drive the reduced H1.8 association to interphase nucleosomes.
source: Altogether, the results suggest that differential positional preferences of H1.8 on the nucleosome (Figure 3A, positioning model) are unlikely to drive the reduced H1.8 association to interphase nucleosomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the structural data presented.

claim: Substantial portions of H1.8 were enriched in sucrose fractions 3 and 4 isolated from interphase chromosomes but not from metaphase chromosomes.
source: Although we could not discern structural differences of H1.8-bound mono-nucleosomes from metaphase and interphase samples, we noticed that substantial portions of H1.8 were enriched in sucrose fractions 3 and 4 isolated from interphase chromosomes but not from metaphase chromosomes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The initial attempt to reconstitute 2D classes of the interphase-specific H1.8-containing complex failed.
source: However, our initial attempt failed to reconstitute any reasonable 2D classes of the interphase-specific H1.8-containing complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is an observation from the initial data processing shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Low S/N ratio particles were not reproducibly recentered during 2D classification.
source: The principle of DuSTER is based on our realization that low S/N ratio particles were not reproducibly recentered during 2D classification (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation that forms the basis of the DuSTER method, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: By setting DTH = 20 Å, 2D classification results were dramatically improved in this sample; a five-petal flower-shaped 2D class was reconstructed.
source: By setting DTH = 20 Å, 2D classification results were dramatically improved in this sample; a five-petal flower-shaped 2D class was reconstructed (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the improved 2D classification results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The particles rejected by DuSTER have a generally weak contrast.
source: As expected, the particles rejected by DuSTER have a generally weak contrast (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by visual evidence in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The selected particles were evenly distributed in all defocus ranges between 1.5 and 3.5 µm.
source: Although higher contrast images can be generated by increasing the defocus (the distance between the target particles and the lens focus), the selected particles were evenly distributed in all defocus ranges between 1.5 and .5 µm (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: 3D DuSTER enabled the reconstruction of 3D structure of the interphase-specific H1.8-containing complex, a pentameric macromolecule with a diameter of approximately 60 Å.
source: 3D DuSTER enabled the reconstruction of 3D structure of the interphase-specific H1.8-containing complex, a pentameric macromolecule with a diameter of approximately 60 Å (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: NPM2 aligned well with the MagIC-cryo-EM result among the proteins detected by MS.
source: To determine the identity of this complex, MagIC-cryo-EM beads used for isolating the complex were analyzed by MS (Figure 4D). Among the proteins detected by MS, NPM2 aligned well with the MagIC-cryo-EM result.
evidence: This is supported by MS data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NPM2 was preferentially enriched in interphase chromatin fractions compared to metaphase.
source: Western blotting confirmed that NPM2 was preferentially enriched in interphase chromatin fractions compared to metaphase (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: NPM2 interacts with H1.8 in chromosome-free egg extracts both in interphase and metaphase.
source: while NPM2 interacts with H1.8 in chromosome-free egg extracts both in interphase and metaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The crystal structure and AlphaFold2-predicted models of Xenopus NPM2 matched the MagIC-cryo-EM structure of the interphase-specific H1.8-bound complex.
source: In addition, the crystal structure and AlphaFold2 (AF2)-predicted models of Xenopus NPM2 matched the MagIC-cryo-EM structure of the interphase-specific H1.8-bound complex (Figure 4F) Dutta et al., 2001.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4F and citation.

claim: NPM2 replaces sperm protamines with core histones upon fertilization in Xenopus eggs, thereby promoting nucleosome assembly on sperm DNA.
source: In Xenopus eggs, NPM2 replaces sperm protamines with core histones upon fertilization, thereby promoting nucleosome assembly on sperm DNA Laskey et al., 1978; Philpott et al., 1991; Ohsumi and Katagiri, 1991.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: NPM2 can extract out somatic linker histones from chromatin.
source: NPM2 can also extract out somatic linker histones from chromatin Dimitrov and Wolffe, 1996; Ramos et al., 2005; Bañuelos et al., 2007.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: X-ray crystallography suggested that recombinant Xenopus NPM2 forms a pentamer and a decamer (a dimer of pentamers).
source: X-ray crystallography suggested that recombinant Xenopus NPM2 forms a pentamer and a decamer (a dimer of pentamers; Dutta et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dutta et al., 2001.

claim: The acidic tracts in the C-terminal tail of NPM2 binds H2A-H2B, histone octamers, and the linker histone H5.
source: The acidic tracts in the C-terminal tail of NPM2 binds H2A-H2B, histone octamers, and the linker histone H5 Platonova et al., 2011; Ramos et al., 2010; Taneva et al., 2009
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Two structural variants of NPM2 bound to H1.8 were identified, classified as open and closed forms.
source: By further analyzing our cryo-EM structure representing the H1.8-bound state of NPM2, we identified two structural variants, classified as open and closed forms (Figure 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 6, and Figure 4—figure supplement 7J–K).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: The major structural differences between the two forms are found at C-terminal and N-terminal segments of NPM2 core and at the A1 loop.
source: The major structural differences between the two forms are found at C-terminal and N-terminal segments of NPM2 core and at the A1 loop (Figures 5 and 6, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: In the closed form, β8 runs straight from the sepal to the petal sides of each pentamer and has an extended C-terminal segment that protrudes past the petal side of the pentamer.
source: In the closed form, β8 runs straight from the sepal to the petal sides of each pentamer and has an extended C-terminal segment that protrudes past the petal side of the pentamer.
evidence: This is a structural description based on the cryo-EM data.

claim: In the open form, the C-terminal portion of β8 is bent outward to the rim.
source: In the open form, however, the C-terminal portion of β8 is bent outward to the rim (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a structural description based on the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Extra cryo-EM densities, which may represent H1.8, are clearly observed in the open form but much less in the closed form near the acidic surface regions proximal to the N terminus of β1 and the C terminus of β8.
source: Notably, extra cryo-EM densities, which may represent H1.8, are clearly observed in the open form but much less in the closed form near the acidic surface regions proximal to the N terminus of β1 and the C terminus of β8 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density maps shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The acidic tract A1 (aa 36–40) and A2 (aa 120–140) respectively interact with and are adjacent to the putative H1.8 density.
source: Supporting this idea, the acidic tract A1 (aa 36–40) and A2 (aa 120–140), which are both implicated in the recognition of basic substrates such as core histones Dutta et al., 2001; Platonova et al., 2011, respectively interact with and are adjacent to the putative H1.8 density (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5B and citations.

claim: The NPM2 surface that is in direct contact with the putative H1.8 density is accessible in the open form while it is internalized in the closed form.
source: In addition, the NPM2 surface that is in direct contact with the putative H1.8 density is accessible in the open form while it is internalized in the closed form (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The size of the NPM2-H1.8 complex estimated from sucrose gradient elution volume is consistent with pentameric NPM2 binding to a single H1.8.
source: As the size of the NPM2-H1.8 complex estimated from sucrose gradient elution volume is consistent with pentameric NPM2 binding to a single H1.8 (Figure 3C and Table 3)
evidence: This is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 3C and Table 3.

claim: Applying C5 symmetry during structural reconstruction likely blurred the density of the monomeric H1.8 that binds to the NPM2 pentamer.
source: applying C5 symmetry during structural reconstruction likely blurred the density of the monomeric H1.8 that binds to the NPM2 pentamer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis and symmetry considerations.

claim: Multiple structural variants of the NPM2 protomer with different degrees of openness co-exist within an NPM2-H1.8 complex.
source: The structural determination of NPM2-H1.8 without applying C5 symmetry lowered the overall resolution but visualized multiple structural variants of the NPM2 protomer with different degrees of openness co-existing within an NPM2-H1.8 complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: MagIC-cryo-EM offers sub-nanometer resolution structural determination using a heterogeneous sample that contains the target molecule at 1~2 nM, which is approximately 100–1000 times lower than the concentration required for conventional cryo-EM methods.
source: MagIC-cryo-EM offers sub-nanometer resolution structural determination using a heterogeneous sample that contains the target molecule at 1~2 nM, which is approximately 100–1000 times lower than the concentration required for conventional cryo-EM methods, including affinity grid approach (Kelly et al., 2008; Llaguno et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of the method's capabilities supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The on-bead-cryo-EM approach minimizes preparation steps, which can lead to sample loss, such as target isolation, enrichment, and buffer exchange.
source: First, the on-bead-cryo-EM approach minimizes preparation steps, which can lead to sample loss, such as target isolation, enrichment, and buffer exchange (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an advantage of the method illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: Sample loss during the grid-freezing process is reduced by magnet-based enrichment of the targets on cryo-EM grids.
source: Second, sample loss during the grid-freezing process is reduced by magnet-based enrichment of the targets on cryo-EM grids (Figures 2E–I–6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2E–I and 6B.

claim: Magnetic beads are easily identifiable on the grid.
source: Third, magnetic beads are easily identifiable on the grid (Figures 2G and 6C).
evidence: This is supported by visual evidence in Figures 2G and 6C.

claim: The target molecules are accumulated around magnetic beads, ensuring that each micrograph contains more than 100 usable particles independent of input sample concentration.
source: Fourth, the target molecules are accumulated around magnetic beads, ensuring that each micrograph contains more than 100 usable particles independent of input sample concentration (Figures 2J and 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2J and 6D.

claim: Particle curation by DuSTER does not require human supervision or machine learning, except for determining the distance threshold between repeatedly picked particles.
source: Notably, particle curation by DuSTER does not require human supervision or machine learning, except for determining the distance threshold between repeatedly picked particles.
evidence: This is a characteristic of the DuSTER method.

claim: The sample requirement for MagIC-cryo-EM is a mere 5 ng per grid, which is comparable to or even lower than the requirements of widely used ChIP-seq.
source: Second, the sample requirement for MagIC-cryo-EM is a mere 5 ng per grid, which is comparable to or even lower than the requirements of widely used ChIP-seq Zou et al., 2022.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison supported by citation.

claim: The majority of chromatin-bound H1.8 in interphase existed as a complex with NPM2 rather than with nucleosomes.
source: Combining MS, MagIC-cryo-EM and DuSTER, we found that the majority of chromatin-bound H1.8 in interphase existed as a complex with NPM2 rather than with nucleosomes (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by MS and structural data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: NPM2 is able to remove linker histones but not core histones from somatic nuclei that are introduced to Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Our observation is also in line with a previous report that NPM2 is able to remove linker histones but not core histones from somatic nuclei that are introduced to Xenopus egg extracts Dimitrov and Wolffe, 1996.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dimitrov and Wolffe, 1996.

claim: The amounts of H1.8-associated NAP1 or NPM2 in the egg cytoplasm did not change between interphase and metaphase.
source: Since the amounts of H1.8-associated NAP1 or NPM2 in the egg cytoplasm did not change between interphase and metaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A mechanism must exist such that NPM2 interacts with H1.8 on chromatin specifically in interphase and suppresses H1.8-nucleosome interaction.
source: a mechanism must exist such that NPM2 interacts with H1.8 on chromatin specifically in interphase and suppresses H1.8-nucleosome interaction (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data, illustrated in Figure 5D.

claim: NPM2 may maintain nucleosome-bound H1.8 at a low level in interphase during early developmental cell cycles to support rapid DNA replication.
source: NPM2 may maintain nucleosome-bound H1.8 at a low level in interphase during early developmental cell cycles to support rapid DNA replication, while mitotic induction of H1.8 association with nucleosomes tunes condensin loading on chromosomes and ensures proper chromosome size to facilitate chromosome segregation (Choppakatla et al., 2021; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the data and supported by citation, illustrated in Figure 5D.

claim: The cryo-EM structure strongly suggests that the NPM2 binds to H1.8 as a homo-pentamer.
source: Our cryo-EM structure strongly suggests that the NPM2 binds to H1.8 as a homo-pentamer.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: The closed form is more similar to the reported crystal structure and AF2-predicted structures, both of which are determined in the absence of the substrates.
source: Since the closed form is more similar to the reported crystal structure and AF2-predicted structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D), both of which are determined in the absence of the substrates
evidence: This is a comparison to prior structures shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Substrate binding induces the structural transition of NPM2 to the open form.
source: our analysis points toward a possibility that substrate binding induces the structural transition of NPM2 to the open form.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The open form provides a stable association platform by exposing the acidic surface at the petal side for the substrate recognition.
source: our data suggest that the open form provides a stable association platform by exposing the acidic surface at the petal side for the substrate recognition
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: The C-terminal A2 and A3 at the flexible tail may facilitate recruitment and possibly also entrapment of the substrate.
source: while the C-terminal A2 and A3 at the flexible tail may facilitate recruitment and possibly also entrapment of the substrate.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: Each NPM2 subunit may independently adapt open and closed form within a pentamer.
source: Since our structural analysis further suggests that each NPM2 subunit may independently adapt open and closed form within a pentamer
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Flexibility in the core domain may enable the association of substrates with diverse sizes and structures to support NPM2's molecular chaperone functionality.
source: this flexibility in the core domain may enable the association of substrates with diverse sizes and structures to support its molecular chaperone functionality.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: Gold grids are suitable for MagIC-cryo-EM, whereas copper grids worsened the final resolution of the structures presumably due to magnetization of the copper grids during the concentration process.
source: We found that gold grids are suitable for MagIC-cryo-EM, whereas copper grids worsened the final resolution of the structures presumably due to magnetization of the copper grids during the concentration process which then interfered with the electron beam and caused the grid to vibrate during data collection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Test 7).
evidence: This is an observation from optimization experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: H1.8-GFP is functional as it rescued the chromosome elongation phenotype caused by H1.8 immunodepletion.
source: We confirmed that H1.8-GFP is functional as it rescued the chromosome elongation phenotype caused by H1.8 immunodepletion (Choppakatla et al., 2021; Maresca et al., 2005; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
